BILINGUAL.EN:
One important problem in designing logic programming languages is that of arranging things so that as few irrelevant query interpreterdata base data baseindexing indexing a data base data-base entries as possible will be examined in checking a given pattern. For this purpose, we will represent an assertion as a list whose head is a string that represents the kind of information of the assertion.
Then, in addition to storing all assertions in one big stream, we store all assertions whose cars are constant symbols in separate streams, in a table indexed by the symbol. To fetch an assertion that may match a pattern, we first check to see if the car of the pattern is a constant symbol. If so, we return (to be tested using the matcher) all the stored assertions that have the same car. If the patterns car is not a constant symbol, we return all the stored assertions. Cleverer methods could also take advantage of information in the frame, or try also to optimize the case where the car of the pattern is not a constant symbol. We avoid building our criteria for indexing (using the car, handling only the case of constant symbols) into the program; instead we call on predicates and selectors that embody our criteria.
We store the assertions in separate streams, one for each kind of information, in a table indexed by the kind. To fetch an assertion that may match a pattern, we return (to be tested using the matcher) all the stored assertions that have the same head (the same kind of information). Cleverer methods could also take advantage of information in the frame. We avoid building our criteria for indexing into the program; instead we call on predicates and selectors that embody our criteria.
